processing: Orthodox black tea. For the frost lots, leaf picked in cold weather goes quickly to the factory and is laid out in withering lofts for an accelerated wither that also thaws it.
harvest_season: Year-round in the usual Nilgiri way, but the prized lot is the winter frost tea, picked around the turn of the year when nights turn freezing.
appearance_dry: Fine, twisted dark leaf with lighter tones in high grades such as SFTGFOP1.
appearance_liquor: Bright, clear golden amber, lighter than an ordinary Nilgiri black.
appearance_wet: Coppery leaf with some green tones, as is common in lightly handled winter teas.
taste_profile: The frost tea is full and rich with a fresh, floral and fruity character, less brisk than a standard Nilgiri cup.

brewing.notes: Western-style. Use slightly cooler water for frost lots so the floral notes stay clean; too hot and long brings out astringency.

vintage_note: The frost tea is sold by year and is labelled as such, for example a 2026 Winter Frost, arriving at importers around February after a winter picking. Quantities are small. Drink it within a year or so, while it is fresh; the estate's other teas follow normal Nilgiri seasonal selling.
description:
Kairbetta is a Nilgiri estate near Kotagiri, known abroad mainly for one thing: its winter frost tea. That makes it a good route into a side of South Indian tea that most people, used to Nilgiri as a blending leaf, never meet.

Frost tea is picked during the cold spell and rushed to withering lofts, where the wither is sped up as the leaf thaws. The aim is a fruity, floral profile that is hard to get in warmer months.

In the cup it is full but fresh, more floral than brisk. Brew it a little cooler and shorter than a regular black tea, and taste before you add anything. Milk would hide what you paid for.

Look for the year and the grade on the label; lots are usually marked SFTGFOP1 and the name may be spelled Kairabetta. Elevation figures vary from one seller to the next, so do not read much into them.
history:
The estate is said to have been founded in 1887 by an Englishman, J.T. Murray, according to the importer Upton Tea, which places it at 6,500 feet near Kotagiri; other sellers give different altitudes. Black tea production began in earnest when a factory was built there in 1926.

Its international profile today comes largely from importers in the United States and Japan who sell its winter frost lots under the estate name.
